title: Normalization layers: LayerNorm to RMSNorm, and why nobody knows why
summary: What a normalization layer does inside a deep network and why the field went from BatchNorm to LayerNorm to RMSNorm, why post-norm needed warmup and pre-norm costs depth, how QK-norm stops attention collapsing to one token, and whether Dynamic Tanh shows the statistics were never the point.

topics: deep dive: normalization layers — LayerNorm to RMSNorm
concepts_taught: normalization layers as subtract-the-mean, divide-by-the-spread plus a learned gain and bias: batch norm averages one unit across the mini-batch (14x fewer steps, but batch-dependent with a separate inference path), layer norm averages across one example's units (identical at train and test, works per time step)

why normalization works is unsettled: internal covariate shift was the founding story, but Santurkar et al.'s injected-noise experiment barely hurt batch norm, pointing instead to a smoother loss landscape; runaway activation growth is a third explanation

RMSNorm drops LayerNorm's re-centering and keeps only re-scaling by the root mean square: identical when the mean is zero, invariant to scaling inputs or weights, an implicit learning-rate governor; 7-64% faster (7-9% on the Transformer, which fails to train with no normalization)

post-norm versus pre-norm placement around the residual connection: post-norm's large output-layer gradients at initialization are why Transformers needed learning-rate warmup (Xiong et al.), pre-norm removes warmup but lets residual-stream variance grow with depth so deep layers act near-identity (the curse of depth), and labs now normalize sublayer outputs too (Gemma 2, OLMo 2)

QK-norm: normalizing queries and keys before the dot product so attention logits cannot grow until softmax goes one-hot (ViT-22B divergence at ~8B), reproducible at small scale with high learning rates (Wortsman et al.), alongside z-loss and logit soft-capping

Dynamic Tanh as a normalization-free replacement: trained layer norms map inputs through tanh-like S-curves, so an element-wise tanh(alpha x) can match normalized Transformers, though LLMs need alpha tuning and compiled code shows no speedup

lore.note: Ada's running cut-list item — the variance argument behind dividing attention scores by the square root of the key dimension, which never survives the term — developed: she framed QK-norm as what happened when that fixed divisor stopped being enough, calling the topic personal.
